slides.headline: 99% female.
slides.sub: Young green turtles from the northern Great Barrier Reef, and warming sand is the reason

slides.headline: The sand decides the sex
slides.body: A sea turtle's sex isn't set at fertilisation. Incubation temperature decides: below 27.7 °C hatchlings are male, above 31 °C female, in between a mix.

slides.headline: Tracing turtles back to their birth beach
slides.body: Researchers used genetics and hormone tests to link green turtles feeding on the Great Barrier Reef to the beaches where they hatched.

slides.headline: Same reef, very different ratios
slides.body: Turtles from cooler southern beaches: 65–69% female. From warmer northern beaches: 99.1% of juveniles, 99.8% of subadults and 86.8% of adults.

slides.label: years the northern beaches have produced mainly females
slides.body: Combining the results with temperature records, the authors warn that complete feminisation of this population is possible in the near future.

slides.headline: Recovering, with a new threat
slides.body: In 2025 the IUCN moved green turtles from Endangered to Least Concern as numbers rose ~28%, thanks to conservation. Warming is a growing threat.

slides.headline: Hot sand, fewer males.
slides.body: Save this for the next climate conversation. Sourced wildlife science, every week.
sources: Jensen, M.P. et al. (2018) Environmental warming and feminization of one of the largest sea turtle populations in the world. Current Biology 28:154–159

IUCN Red List: Chelonia mydas (assessed 2024, published 2025)

caption:
Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) hatchlings get their sex from sand temperature, and warmer beaches mean more females.

A green turtle lays about 110 eggs per nest, and they incubate in the sand for about two months, so a hotter summer can tip a whole season's hatchlings towards female. On the northern Great Barrier Reef, that tip has lasted more than two decades.

Swipe for the numbers. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Jensen et al. (2018), Current Biology; NOAA; IUCN Red List (2025).
